title: The HPV vaccine: what it protects against and who it is for
intro: The human papillomavirus vaccine protects against infection with the types of HPV that most often cause cervical cancer and several other cancers, as well as genital warts. Vaccination is recommended in many countries for children and adolescents before they become sexually active. Understanding how it works helps families make an informed decision.

sections.heading: What HPV vaccines protect against
paragraphs: HPV is a very common virus group spread through skin and mucous membrane contact, mostly during sex. Most infections clear without symptoms, but certain high-risk types can persist and cause changes that develop into cancer of the cervix, anus, vulva, vagina, penis or throat. Other types cause genital warts.

Current vaccines protect against the most important high-risk types, and some also against the types that cause most genital warts. They prevent infection, but they do not treat an existing infection.

sections.heading: Who is recommended to be vaccinated
paragraphs: Vaccination is usually recommended for girls and boys at around nine to fourteen years of age, ideally before the first sexual contact. Vaccination at this age produces a strong immune response and often needs only two doses given several months apart. People who start later usually need three doses.
Many countries offer catch-up vaccination up to young adulthood. Adults beyond the recommended ages may still benefit, depending on their past exposure, and should discuss this with their doctor.

sections.heading: Safety and side effects
paragraphs: HPV vaccines have been studied in very large groups worldwide. Common reactions are pain, redness or swelling at the injection site, headache, tiredness and mild fever, which usually pass within a few days. Fainting can occur after any injection, so it is sensible to sit for a few minutes afterwards.
Serious allergic reactions are very rare. Monitoring systems continue to watch safety, and health authorities have not found evidence of a link to long-term illnesses that were once feared.

sections.heading: Vaccination and screening
paragraphs: The vaccine does not protect against every cancer-causing type, so women should still take part in regular cervical screening after vaccination. Condoms reduce but do not fully prevent HPV transmission.
Evidence shows that vaccination programmes have markedly lowered rates of precancerous changes and, in some countries, of cervical cancer in vaccinated groups.

sections.heading: Practical points
paragraphs: Check local recommendations and which costs are covered by health insurance. Keep your vaccination record safe, and ask about timing relative to other vaccines. If your child is unwell with fever, the vaccination can usually be postponed.

examples.title: Making a family decision
examples.text: Imagine your twelve-year-old is eligible for the HPV vaccine. You could read about benefits and side effects, write down your questions, and talk through them with your paediatrician before deciding together.

examples.title: Catching up as a young adult
examples.text: Suppose you are 22 and were never vaccinated. You might ask whether catch-up is recommended for you, how many doses are needed and whether it is still helpful if you have already been sexually active.
